title: The Demon Ministers' Counsel
story:
Kamsa had killed every child his sister Devaki had borne, and still the fear that drove him would not loosen its grip. All through the night it lay on his chest like a stone, and when the darkness at last began to thin he did what a frightened king does: he reached for counsel. He summoned his ministers to the palace in Mathura, and they came to him before dawn. The fear had a name, though he could not bring himself to say it aloud — the prophecy that Devaki's eighth child would one day take his life.

The men who gathered around him were no ordinary courtiers. They were the enemies of the gods, demons who had insinuated themselves into his court and who fed, as such creatures do, on fear. Their hatred of heaven was older than his own, an enmity stretched back through the ages, and it made them, of all his counselors, the most eager to see the earth stripped of its holy things. The king had never lacked for flatterers, but what he needed now was counsel, and these were the ones who could give it — because they wanted what he wanted, only more so. They watched their king pace the torchlit hall, listened while he poured out the dread he could no longer contain, and when he had done they gave him their answer.

Do not fear the gods on the field of battle, they told him. When your arrows rain down on them from every side, what do they do? They turn and run. They cast away their weapons, forget the arts of war they once knew, and stand with their hands folded, wretched and pleading, their chariots lost and their courage gone. Some weep; some beg with folded palms. Men who are brave only while there is peace, who boast loudly and melt at the first clash — what is there in such creatures to dread?

And yet, the ministers went on, do not think them harmless. A sickness that is ignored while it is still small, left to take root in the body, can never be cured once it has spread through the limbs. The gods are the same. Leave them in peace, and they will gather their strength in secret and return, stronger than they were before. The enemy you think you have already beaten will rise again from the very places you never think to look.

Because the gods have a root, and the root is Vishnu. Wherever eternal dharma stands, wherever men hold fast to the truth, there Vishnu dwells. The gods do not draw their life from swords or armies or walls. They draw it from the holy: from the brahmanas who know Brahman, from the cows, from the Vedas, from austerity and truth, from self-control and tranquillity. The enemy of the asuras does not stand in the open where an arrow might reach him. He hides in these things, in the quiet heart of every good and simple life, and while a single one of them remains, the gods remain.

So cut the root, O king. Slay the newborn in every city and village. Root out the brahmanas, the cows, the Vedas, every act of penance and every honest word. Starve the gods of all they live on, and the enemy you fear will have nothing left to stand on.

Kamsa listened, and the counsel settled into him the way cold water sinks into dry ground. He had spent the night afraid of one child, of one prophecy; now the fear had a shape, and a plan to match it. In that room, spoken into his fear by the enemies of the gods, the decision was made. The torches guttered, and no one in that hall spoke the word mercy.
reflection: The ministers' counsel is chilling because buried inside it is one true observation: the gods cannot be beaten by arms, only by destroying the dharma in which they dwell. Their remedy is fear made policy, the logic of a man who would burn the whole field to kill one weed.
content_note: Kamsa's ministers urge the slaughter of infants and of the holy; the violence is counselled, not shown.
next_story_tease: And Kamsa, having heard them, did not delay in carrying the counsel out.
hero_scene: Kamsa on his throne in the torchlit hall at night while his demon ministers lean in around him, urging him to slay every infant and to root out the brahmanas, the cows and the rites in which the gods keep their life.
visual_elements: images of gods fleeing, weapons cast down
